Control cache size with [`cacheMaxMemorySize`](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/incrementalCacheHandlerPath). | 208 209 For example, in a serverless environment, a cached function shared by two pages executes on each static shell revalidation, whereas in self-hosted or environments with persistent memory, the cached output is reused if it's still fresh. 210 211 If the default in-memory cache isn't enough, consider **[`use cache: remote`](/docs/app/api-reference/directives/use-cache-remote)** which allows platforms to provide a dedicated cache handler (like Redis or KV database). {shared.current}
262 } 263 ``` 264 265 This isolation ensures cached functions have predictable, self-contained behavior. It should be used alongside the [`use cache`](/docs/app/api-reference/directives/use-cache) directive, and within the scope of the function or component. 15 16 ## Usage 17 18 ### Basic setup 19 20 To use `cacheLife`, first enable the [`cacheComponents` flag](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheComponents) in your `next.config.js` file: 21 22 ```ts filename="next.config.ts" switcher 23 import type { NextConfig } from 'next' 24 25 const nextConfig: NextConfig = { 26 cacheComponents: true, 27 } 28 29 export default nextConfig 30 ``` 31 32 ```js filename="next.config.js" switcher 33 const nextConfig = { 34 cacheComponents: true, 35 } 36 37 export default nextConfig 38 ``` 39 40 `cacheLife` can only be used within a cache directive scope. 41 42 Add a cache directive (for example, `use cache`) at the file level or at the top of an async function or component. 43 44 `cacheLife` cannot be used at module scope. Calling it at the top level of a file will throw an error. 45 46 > **Good to know**: 47 > 48 > - Calling `cacheLife` is optional. If omitted, a default cache lifetime is applied. 49 > - Call `cacheLife` in the same function or component where caching is defined. Avoid abstracting it into shared utilities so the cache behavior remains explicit and easy to reason about. 50 > - If you call `cacheLife`, ensure only one call executes per function invocation. You can call it in different control flow branches, but only one should run per request. See the [conditional cache lifetimes](#conditional-cache-lifetimes) example. 51 52 ### Using preset profiles 53 54 Next.js provides preset cache profiles that cover common caching needs. Each profile balances three factors: 55 56 - How long users see cached content without checking for updates (client-side) 57 - How often fresh content is generated on the server 58 - When old content expires completely 59 60 Choose a profile based on how frequently your content changes: 61 62 - **`seconds`** - Real-time data (stock prices, live scores) 63 - **`minutes`** - Frequently updated (social feeds, news) 64 - **`hours`** - Multiple daily updates (product inventory, weather) 65 - **`days`** - Daily updates (blog posts, articles) 66 - **`weeks`** - Weekly updates (podcasts, newsletters) 67 - **`max`** - Rarely changes (legal pages, archived content) 68 69 Import `cacheLife` and pass a profile name: 70 71 ```tsx filename="app/blog/page.tsx" highlight={1,5} 72 'use cache' 73 import { cacheLife } from 'next/cache' 74 75 export default async function BlogPage() { 76 cacheLife('days') // Blog content updated daily 77 78 const posts = await getBlogPosts() 79 return
{/* render posts */}
80 } 81 ``` 82 83 The profile name tells Next.js how to cache the entire function's output. If you don't call `cacheLife`, the `default` profile is used. See [preset cache profiles](#preset-cache-profiles) for timing details. 84 85 ## Reference 86 87 ### Cache profile properties 88 89 Cache profiles control caching behavior through three timing properties: 90 91 - **[`stale`](#stale)**: How long the client can use cached data without checking the server 92 - **[`revalidate`](#revalidate)**: After this time, the next request will trigger a background refresh 93 - **[`expire`](#expire)**: After this time with no requests, the next one waits for fresh content 94 95 #### `stale` 96 97 **Client-side:** How long the client can use cached data without checking the server. 98 99 During this time, the client-side router displays cached content immediately without any network request. After this period expires, the router must check with the server on the next navigation or request. This provides instant page loads from the client cache, but data may be outdated. 100 101 - If omitted, defaults to the `default` profile's `stale` value (5 minutes, see [`staleTimes`](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/staleTimes)) 102 103 ```tsx 104 cacheLife({ stale: 300 }) // 5 minutes 105 ``` 106 107 #### `revalidate` 108 109 How often the server regenerates cached content in the background. 110 111 - When a request arrives after this period, the server: 112 1. Serves the cached version immediately (if available) 113 2. Regenerates content in the background 114 3. Updates the cache with fresh content 115 - Similar to [Incremental Static Regeneration (ISR)](/docs/app/guides/incremental-static-regeneration) 116 - If omitted, defaults to the `default` profile's `revalidate` value (15 minutes) 117 118 ```tsx 119 cacheLife({ revalidate: 900 }) // 15 minutes 120 ``` 121 122 #### `expire` 123 124 Maximum time before the server must regenerate cached content. 125 126 - After this period with no traffic, the server regenerates content synchronously on the next request 127 - When you set both `revalidate` and `expire`, `expire` must be longer than `revalidate`. Next.js validates this and raises an error for invalid configurations. 128 - If omitted, defaults to the `default` profile's `expire` value (never expires) 129 130 ```tsx 131 cacheLife({ expire: 3600 }) // 1 hour 132 ``` 133 134 ### Preset cache profiles 135 136 If you don't specify a profile, Next.js uses the `default` profile. We recommend explicitly setting a profile to make caching behavior clear. 137 138 | **Profile** | **Use Case** | `stale` | `revalidate` | `expire` | 139 | ----------- | -------------------------------------- | ---------- | ------------ | -------- | 140 | `default` | Standard content | 5 minutes | 15 minutes | never | 141 | `seconds` | Real-time data | 30 seconds | 1 second | 1 minute | 142 | `minutes` | Frequently updated content | 5 minutes | 1 minute | 1 hour | 143 | `hours` | Content updated multiple times per day | 5 minutes | 1 hour | 1 day | 144 | `days` | Content updated daily | 5 minutes | 1 day | 1 week | 145 | `weeks` | Content updated weekly | 5 minutes | 1 week | 30 days | 146 | `max` | Stable content that rarely changes | 5 minutes | 30 days | 1 year | 147 148 ### Custom cache profiles 149 150 Define reusable cache profiles in your `next.config.ts` file: 151 152 ```ts filename="next.config.ts" 153 import type { NextConfig } from 'next' 154 155 const nextConfig: NextConfig = { 156 cacheComponents: true, 157 cacheLife: { 158 biweekly: { 159 stale: 60 * 60 * 24 * 14, // 14 days 160 revalidate: 60 * 60 * 24, // 1 day 161 expire: 60 * 60 * 24 * 14, // 14 days 162 }, 163 }, 164 } 165 166 export default nextConfig 167 ``` 168 169 ```js filename="next.config.js" switcher 170 const nextConfig = { 171 cacheComponents: true, 172 cacheLife: { 173 biweekly: { 174 stale: 60 * 60 * 24 * 14, // 14 days 175 revalidate: 60 * 60 * 24, // 1 day 176 expire: 60 * 60 * 24 * 14, // 14 days 177 }, 178 }, 179 } 180 181 module.exports = nextConfig 182 ``` 183 184 The example above caches for 14 days, checks for updates daily, and expires the cache after 14 days. You can then reference this profile throughout your application by its name: 185 186 > **Good to know**: Any omitted properties in a custom profile inherit from the `default` profile. This also applies to inline profile objects passed directly to `cacheLife()`. 187 188 ```tsx filename="app/page.tsx" highlight={5} 189 'use cache' 190 import { cacheLife } from 'next/cache' 191 192 export default async function Page() { 193 cacheLife('biweekly') 194 return
Page
195 } 196 ``` 197 198 ### Overriding the default cache profiles 199 200 While the default cache profiles provide a useful way to think about how fresh or stale any given part of cacheable output can be, you may prefer different named profiles to better align with your applications caching strategies. 201 202 You can override the default named cache profiles by creating a new configuration with the same name as the defaults. 203 204 The example below shows how to override the default `"days"` cache profile: 205 206 ```ts filename="next.config.ts" 207 const nextConfig = { 208 cacheComponents: true, 209 cacheLife: { 210 // Override the 'days' profile 211 days: { 212 stale: 3600, // 1 hour 213 revalidate: 900, // 15 minutes 214 expire: 86400, // 1 day 215 }, 216 }, 217 } 218 219 export default nextConfig 220 ``` 221 222 ### Inline cache profiles 223 224 For one-off cases, pass a profile object directly to `cacheLife`: 225 226 ```tsx filename="app/page.tsx" 227 'use cache' 228 import { cacheLife } from 'next/cache' 229 230 export default async function Page() { 231 cacheLife({ 232 stale: 3600, 233 revalidate: 900, 234 expire: 86400, 235 }) 236 237 return
Page
238 } 239 ``` 240 241 Inline profiles apply only to the specific function or component. For reusable configurations, define custom profiles in `next.config.ts`. 242 243 Using `cacheLife({})` with an empty object applies the `default` profile values. 244 245 ### Client cache behavior 246 247 The `stale` property controls the [Client Cache](/docs/app/glossary#client-cache), not the `Cache-Control` header: 248 249 - The server sends the stale time via the `x-nextjs-stale-time` response header 250 - The client router uses this value to determine when to revalidate 251 - **Minimum of 30 seconds is enforced** to ensure prefetched links remain usable 252 253 This 30-second minimum prevents prefetched data from expiring before users can click on links. Static parts are prerendered, while short-lived caches create boundaries where data is fetched at request time rather than build time. Use a `` boundary around dynamic caches to provide a fallback while content loads. 264 265 ## Examples 266 267 ### Using preset profiles 268 269 The simplest way to configure caching is using preset profiles. {post.content}
280 } 281 ``` 282 283 ```tsx filename="app/products/[id]/page.tsx" 284 import { cacheLife } from 'next/cache' 285 286 export default async function ProductPage() { 287 'use cache' 288 cacheLife('hours') // Product data updated multiple times per day 289 290 const product = await fetchProduct() 291 return
{product.name}
292 } 293 ``` 294 295 ### Custom profiles for specific needs 296 297 Define custom profiles when preset options don't match your requirements: 298 299 ```ts filename="next.config.ts" 300 import type { NextConfig } from 'next' 301 302 const nextConfig: NextConfig = { 303 cacheComponents: true, 304 cacheLife: { 305 editorial: { 306 stale: 600, // 10 minutes 307 revalidate: 3600, // 1 hour 308 expire: 86400, // 1 day 309 }, 310 marketing: { 311 stale: 300, // 5 minutes 312 revalidate: 1800, // 30 minutes 313 expire: 43200, // 12 hours 314 }, 315 }, 316 } 317 318 export default nextConfig 319 ``` EditorialPage() { 327 'use cache' 328 cacheLife('editorial') 329 // ... 330 } 331 ``` 332 333 ### Inline profiles for unique cases 334 335 Use inline profiles when a specific function needs one-off 'use cache' 343 344 cacheLife({ 345 stale: 60, // 1 minute 346 revalidate: 300, // 5 minutes 347 expire: 3600, // 1 hour 348 }) 349 350 const offer = await getDb().offer.findFirst({ 351 where: { type: 'limited' }, 352 orderBy: { created_at: 'desc' }, 353 }) 354 355 return offer 356 } 357 358 export async function GET() { 359 const offer = await getLimitedOffer() 360 361 return Response.json(offer) 362 } 363 ``` 364 365 ### Caching individual functions 366 367 Apply caching to utility functions for granular control: 368 369 ```tsx filename="lib/api.ts" 370 import { cacheLife } from 'next/cache' {/* render posts */}
80 } 81 ``` 82 83 The profile name tells Next.js how to cache the entire function's output. If you don't call `cacheLife`, the `default` profile is used. 14	
15	The `cacheTag` function allows you to tag cached data for on-demand invalidation. By associating tags with cache entries, you can selectively purge or revalidate specific cache entries without affecting other cached data.
16	
17	## Usage
18	
19	To use `cacheTag`, enable the [`cacheComponents` flag](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheComponents) in your `next.config.js` file:
20	
21	```ts filename="next.config.ts" switcher
22	import type { NextConfig } from 'next'
23	
24	const nextConfig: NextConfig = {
25	  cacheComponents: true,
26	}
27	
28	export default nextConfig
29	```
30	
31	```js filename="next.config.js" switcher
32	const nextConfig = {
33	  cacheComponents: true,
34	}
35	
36	export default nextConfig
37	```
38	
39	The `cacheTag` function takes one or more string values.
40	
41	```tsx filename="app/data.ts" switcher
42	import { cacheTag } from 'next/cache'
43	
44	export async function getData() {
45	  'use cache'
46	  cacheTag('my-data')
47	  const data = await fetch('/api/data')
48	  return data
49	}
50	```
51	
52	```jsx filename="app/data.js" switcher
53	import { cacheTag } from 'next/cache'
54	
55	export async function getData() {
56	  'use cache'
57	  cacheTag('my-data')
58	  const data = await fetch('/api/data')
59	  return data
60	}
61	```
62	
63	You can then purge the cache on-demand from a [Server Function](/docs/app/getting-started/mutating-data) or [Route Handler](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/route):
64	
65	- Use [`updateTag`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/updateTag) inside a Server Function for read-your-own-writes scenarios, where a user makes a change and the next read should fetch fresh data immediately.
66	- Use [`revalidateTag`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/revalidateTag) when it is acceptable to serve stale data while revalidation happens in the background, or when revalidating from a route handler.
67	
68	The example below uses `revalidateTag`:
69	
70	```tsx filename="app/action.ts" switcher
71	'use server'
72	
73	import { revalidateTag } from 'next/cache'
74	
75	export default async function submit() {
76	  await addPost()
77	  revalidateTag('my-data', 'max')
78	}
79	```
80	
81	```jsx filename="app/action.js" switcher

## Summary

This project uses **Next.js 16**, where the modern caching approach is the **`use cache` directive** (the Cache Components feature) — not `fetch`-level `revalidate` or `unstable_cache` from older versions.

**`next.config.ts`** — enabled the required flag:
```ts
cacheComponents: true  // required for `use cache`, cacheLife, and cacheTag
```

**`app/page.tsx`** — converted to an async cached Server Component:
- `'use cache'` marks the component cacheable.
- `cacheLife({ revalidate: 3600 })` sets the **1-hour cache duration** (`stale`/`expire` inherit from the `default` profile).
- `cacheTag('posts')` tags the entry so it can be invalidated **on-demand** from a Server Action or Route Handler via `revalidateTag('posts')` (or `updateTag('posts')` for read-your-own-writes).
- `await getPosts()` fetches the posts, rendered as a list.

A couple of notes on choices I made:
- I used an **inline `cacheLife({ revalidate: 3600 })`** rather than the preset `cacheLife('hours')` because the `hours` preset revalidates at 1h but expires at 1 day with a 5-min stale — the inline form maps precisely to "1 hour cache duration." Easy to switch to a named profile if you prefer.
- To actually invalidate on-demand, you'll add a Server Action/Route Handler calling `revalidateTag('posts')` when posts change — that piece lives wherever your mutations happen, so I didn't add it here.
